ADDISON TIMES MAJOR SPONSOR: STEPHENSON RIFE ATTORNEYS
Fairland Senior Services marks 12 years of building community
For Kathy Miller, the weekly gatherings at Fairland’s Horizon Center, a program of Shelby Senior Services, provide residents with an inexpensive lunch and a place to play cards, but more importantly, a sense of purpose.
“The thing about this group is it has truly become a family,” said Miller, coordinator of the center. “They are so concerned about one another. They check on one another all the time. If somebody’s not here, somebody knows why.”
The program will celebrate its 12th anniversary Sunday, Sept. 13, with a community fundraiser at the Fairland Volunteer Fire Department. Organizers are preparing for as many as 300 people.
The event will run from 4:30 to 7:15 p.m. and feature a free concert by Terry Lee Ridley and his Million Dollar Band beginning at 6 p.m. Ridley, whose performances draw upon the music and showmanship of Elvis Presley and Jerry Lee Lewis, also performed at the celebration two years ago.
Food will be served from 4:30 to 6:15 p.m., including hamburgers, hot dogs, coney dogs, coleslaw, chips, desserts and drinks. The Fairland Lions Club will provide ice cream.
There is no admission charge, and food will be offered for a freewill donation. Proceeds will remain with the Fairland program.
“We don’t want anyone who might want to just see what’s going on feel like it’s going to cost them or they have to get a ticket,” Miller said. “It’s a celebration.”
The event will be held inside the fire station bays, rain or shine. Tables and chairs will be available, although attendees may bring lawn chairs. With a large crowd anticipated, Fairland Christian Church and Grace Community Church are making their parking lots available. Hometown Hop On will provide golf-cart transportation between parking areas and the fire station.
Miller said the annual celebration began as a way to introduce residents to the new senior program in a welcoming setting. It has since become both a fundraiser and an opportunity for people who have never attended a weekly gathering to learn what the center offers.
She recalled one woman who first came to an anniversary celebration without many connections in Fairland. With few exceptions for medical needs and vacations, the woman has since attended every Thursday and now helps organize the center’s games.
“She tells me over and over what a great thing that has been for her life,” Miller said. “She’s just blossomed, and she has friends that she hadn’t even dreamed about having. Those are the good stories. Those are the things that make me keep going back.”
The Fairland program meets each Thursday and has recently served more than 50 people for lunch each week. Meals cost $5, with Miller cooking some weeks and arranging catered meals at other times. Participants regularly provide desserts, help serve, wash dishes and clean the facility.
That willingness to contribute was especially apparent during the center’s Christmas in July collection. Participants donated more than $2,000 worth of supplies, including paper products, cleaning materials, food-storage bags, coffee creamer and even fluorescent lightbulbs after one member noticed that lights in the facility needed to be replaced.
“They’re not coming there expecting something,” Miller said. “They’re coming there to be part of something that’s good for everybody.”
The center also offers fitness and wellness activities, educational presentations, Bible studies, games, crafts, entertainment and trips. Seniors and their families can receive assistance with issues involving Medicare, caregiving, health care decisions, elder abuse and other challenges. ShelbyGo provides transportation services.
The educational offerings sometimes address subjects families may find difficult to discuss. Miller said 35 people recently remained after lunch for a presentation on hospice and palliative care, asking questions for more than an hour.
“When you can sit down and talk about those things together, then it’s different,” she said. “You’re not doing it alone. You can hear about someone else’s experience in a setting that feels like home.”
Miller said that mission has become more personal since the death of her husband two years ago. She had long understood that the center was important for widows and widowers, but the experience gave her a new appreciation for what a shared meal and regular conversation can mean.
“The social part is so important,” she said. “They can sit down and have lunch with somebody one day a week, and they can have a conversation about the news or about what’s going on in their life. It’s just that connection back to a relationship.”
The center also gives its participants opportunities to contribute to the wider Fairland community. Miller said local leaders seek seniors’ views about the town and its future, while the Town of Fairland demonstrated its support with a $4,500 commitment to the anniversary fundraiser.
“Everybody needs to feel like they have a purpose, and that’s what the senior center gives them,” Miller said. “Somebody’s depending on them. Somebody’s going to miss them if they’re not there. Somebody’s going to reach out and find out what’s wrong.”
Miller credited the center’s participants, volunteers, the Fairland Volunteer Fire Department and Shelby Senior Services staff with making the anniversary event possible.
“It takes the town of Fairland,” she said. “It’s a group effort to put this event on.”
For more information, contact Miller at 317-364-0029.

The following building permits were filed last month in Shelbyville: a new convenience store and gas station canopy for Wawa at 825 E. State Road 44; remodel an area of the existing hospital for a pediatric therapy gym at 2451 Intelliplex Dr.; a new storage shed at 513 Tom Van Arden Dr.; a roof over an existing area at Blue River Cross Country on Lee Blvd.; an outdoor pavilion at 1305 Breckinridge Way; a sunroom addition at 197 Randell Court; enclose a portion of an existing carport, 901 Hemlock St.; remodel bathroom at Sandman Brothers, 56 E. Broadway St.; and construction of 18 new homes.
Dr. Todd Hitchcock, who is stepping down after seven years as superintendent of Shelby Eastern Schools, has been named executive director of the Indiana Construction Roundtable Foundation. Hitchcock, who has served on the foundation’s board for 2½ years, will begin Oct. 1 and focus on strengthening connections among schools, employers and careers in construction and the skilled trades.
The MHP Wound Center will hold its sixth annual Healing Hustle 5K Run/Walk on Saturday, Sept. 19, on Intelliplex Drive in Shelbyville. Bib pickup will begin at 8 a.m., followed by the race at 9 a.m. The Kids Fun Run for children 12 and younger is at 10 a.m. Participants may run or walk, and community members are also invited to attend and cheer for those taking part.
Registration is available online here.The Joseph Boggs Society Museum will be open Sunday, Sept. 13, 1 to 4 p.m.
ANNIVERSARY ANNOUNCEMENT: Steve and Karen (Bush) Runnebohm celebrate 32 years of marriage today. The Runnebohms have four children, seven grandchildren and three great-grandchildren.
HOOSIER NEWS: A proposed $16 million, 124-room Atwell Suites hotel in Fishers is moving forward after a nearly two-year delay prompted by neighborhood objections and city concerns about its original design. The four-story hotel has been relocated to a nearly 2-acre parcel at East 134th Street and Olio Road in the Saxony area and redesigned with brick, fiber cement board, porcelain tile and two public art murals. City staff has recommended approval, subject to revisions involving parking, landscaping and right-of-way plans; if completed, it would be Indiana’s first Atwell Suites. (IBJ)
NATIONAL NEWS: Some libraries have begun organizing materials by topic, similar to bookstores, rather than relying exclusively on the Dewey Decimal System. Deschutes County, Oregon, began testing the approach in 2017 by reorganizing children’s picture books by topic instead of alphabetically by author, resulting in a 20% increase in circulation; reorganizing the law library led to a 10% increase. After the system expanded the approach to all its libraries, the average share of materials checked out at a given time rose from 20% to nearly 30%, while circulation of adult nonfiction increased from 15% to 27%. (Fast Company/Numlock)

This Day in Shelby County History
Local headlines reported on or around this date in Shelby County history. Selections are curated by The Addison Times from Shelby County Public Library Genealogy Department materials. | research by MYRON RAWLINGS
2006: Cossairt Flowers and Freeman Family Funeral Homes sponsored a local edition of Good Neighbor Day. Those who brought a nonperishable food item to Cossairt Florist received 12 gerbera daisies, one to keep and 11 to share.
1996: During Shelby County Council budget sessions, Judge Charles O’Connor discussed the possibility of saving $10,000 a year on law books by investing in a computerized law library.
1986: Knauf Fiber Glass announced plans to build a $5 million, 230,000-square-foot warehouse at its local factory. The company employed 735 people in Shelbyville.
1976: Shelbyville’s Kevin Siebert led the 32-car Pro Comp qualifying field at the U.S. Nationals at Indianapolis Raceway Park. Kevin, 21, was the son of local Oldsmobile dealer Don Siebert.
1966: The SHS football team prepared to open the season at Madison Heights of Anderson. The likely lineup would be Steve Drake, Steve Zeller, Barry Shambach, Kip Kiser, Pete Hall, John Chesser, Larry Lewis, Ron Winton, Ron Brown, Mike Platt and Kevin Avant on offense. On defense, the lineup included several offensive players and Bob Ewing, Wes Miller, Mike McKee and Rex Steffey.
1956: Twelve young men from the region enlisted in the Navy’s high school graduate training program and left for Great Lakes, Illinois. They were Gene Weaver, Donald Hewitt, Joseph Stagge, Marion Fenley Jr., Loren Thoman, Larry Killen, Ted Hodson, Gary Jones, Joseph Keaton, James Friddle, Donald Kuhn and Lowell Vogel.
1946: Karl Kennedy, of Shelbyville, served as installing officer for a “colored” American Legion post in Franklin.
1936: Jimmie Goodwin, described in local papers as “the last of the human bats,” performed during the air circus at the Shelbyville municipal airport. “Leaving the ship at an altitude of 10,000 feet, the ‘Human Bat’ wearing a suit resembling the wings of a bat will soar, spin, glide and loop until he reaches an altitude of 1,000 feet. Here he releases his ‘chute’ and floats to the ground,” The Republican said.
1926: The Shelbyville Candy Kitchen, previously located on North Harrison Street, moved into a store just west of Woolworth’s.
Lucinda Query, who lived at the corner of Broadway and Tompkins streets, celebrated her 95th birthday.

OBITUARIES
Janice Elizabeth Fuller Krebs—although you would have been hard-pressed to find anyone who called her Janice—was known simply as Betty. She died peacefully on August 28, 2026, in Indianapolis. Born March 22, 1941, in Shelbyville, Indiana, to Everett and Margaret (Treon) Fuller, Betty was the third of six children and the only girl, growing up surrounded by five brothers. Perhaps that explains both her lifelong love of sports and her ability to hold her own in just about any situation.
Betty graduated from Shelbyville High School in 1959, where she was a baton-twirling majorette. After graduation, she moved to Indianapolis and began a career that would span several very different chapters. After working at Major Hospital in Shelbyville, she spent 24 years at Thornton Haymond Medical Lab before beginning the part of her career for which generations of families would remember her best: serving as the beloved front-office secretary at Butler Preschool and later Sycamore School. She retired from Sycamore in 2012, although “retirement” never meant slowing down very much. Betty met the love of her life, Jack Krebs, while they were students at Shelbyville High School. Their road to happily-ever-after wasn’t entirely direct. After a break, their families decided the two clearly belonged together and helped nudge them back in the right direction. Apparently, their families knew what they were doing. Betty and Jack married on August 8, 1975. Their relationship ultimately spanned more than six decades—a life built around family, friends, sports, travel, and an extraordinary number of games played in gyms, stadiums, and arenas across the country.
To say Betty was a sports fan would be an understatement. She loved Indiana University basketball and football and was there for the Hoosiers’ first Rose Bowl appearance in 1968. Butler athletics became an equally important part of Betty and Jack’s lives. If Butler was playing football, volleyball, men’s basketball, or women’s basketball, there was a very good chance Betty and Jack were there. Home games were only the beginning. They traveled with friends—and sometimes with the teams—to away games, tournaments, NCAA appearances, and countless other events. Some people plan vacations around beaches. Betty planned them around schedules. Her adventures weren’t limited to sports. In 1974, Betty was named National Ms. Singleton, an honor that gave her opportunities to travel throughout the United States and overseas. It was one of many chapters in a life that was far more interesting than Betty was ever likely to make a fuss about.
Betty and Jack’s greatest investment, however, was always family. They proudly supported their daughter, Courtney, in seemingly every endeavor, including helping to found Sycamore School. Years later, Betty and Courtney even spent more than eight years working together in Sycamore’s front office—a mother-daughter arrangement that surely produced enough stories for an obituary all its own. When Courtney was dancing, Betty was there, too. She spent countless hours driving to lessons, rehearsals, and performances, usually with a camera nearby. Over the years she took hundreds—more accurately, probably thousands—of photographs and carefully assembled albums filled with practices, performances, and candid moments. Together, they became a photographic history of Courtney’s dancing years and a lasting example of one of the ways Betty loved best: by being there, paying attention, and remembering the details.
For years, Betty was also quite clear that she didn’t “do babies.” Then her grandson, Jackson, was born. The rule was promptly abandoned. Betty loved being his Gamma. She treasured their time together, whether she was picking him up from school, spending an afternoon with him, or simply enjoying the privilege of watching him grow. Jackson occupied a place in Betty’s heart that made her previous policy on babies seem particularly negotiable.
Betty was preceded in death by her parents, Everett and Margaret Fuller; her brothers Jim, David, Tim, and Danny Fuller; her in-laws, Freeman and Millie Krebs; and her sister- and brother-in-law, Donna and Bill Dietz. She is survived by Jack, her husband and partner in more than 60 years of adventures; her daughter and son-in-law, Courtney and Ian Henderson; her grandson, Jackson; her brother and sister-in-law, Reggie and Christine Fuller; and her aunt, Peggy Elsbury. She also leaves behind countless nieces and nephews, cousins, dear friends, former coworkers, students, and families—and a remarkable number of people whose lives became connected to hers through Shelbyville, Butler, Indiana University, Sycamore School, and all the places in between.
Private graveside services will be observed by the family. But a quiet goodbye alone wouldn’t be quite right for Betty. Instead, family and friends are invited to a Celebration of Betty’s Life on Sunday, September 13, from 3-5 pm at Hinkle Fieldhouse on the campus of Butler University. In keeping with Betty’s spirit, please leave the formal mourning clothes at home and come wearing your Butler, IU, Shelbyville, or Sycamore best. Team colors, school gear, and good stories are encouraged. Please RSVP and share your favorite stories, memories, and photographs of Betty here: Celebration of Betty’s Life- RSVP and Memories. Whether or not you are able to attend the celebration, the family would love to have your memories and photographs as they remember and celebrate Betty’s life. In lieu of flowers, the family invites those wishing to remember Betty to make a contribution to Butler University’s Bulldog Club in honor of Betty Krebs or to a charity of your choice. Gifts to the Butler Bulldog Club in honor of Betty Krebs may be made online at https://give.butler.edu/give/481721#!/donation/checkout. Check the “in honor or memory of” box and select “Bulldog Club” from the drop-down menu. Gifts by check should be made payable to Butler University, with “Bulldog Club/Betty Krebs” written in the memo line, and mailed to: Butler Athletics, Attn: Bulldog Club, 510 W. 49th Street, Indianapolis, Indiana 46208. For additional information about making a gift, please contact the Bulldog Club at 317-940-6253 or bulldogclub@butler.edu. Betty’s life was filled with the things she loved: family, friendships, schools that became communities, teams worth cheering for, places worth traveling to, and moments worth photographing. While we grieve the loss of Betty from our lives, let us not be defined by tears, but instead remember the stories, the memories, and her bright, unforgettable smile.
Craig Ronald Sethman, 46, of Shelbyville, passed away unexpectedly Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Craig was born Oct. 12, 1979, in Washington, Pennsylvania, and came to Shelbyville with his family at a young age. He was baptized in the Russian Orthodox Church. He graduated from Shelbyville High School in 1998 and continued his education at Ivy Tech Community College, where he earned his associate degree and journeyman electrician certification. Craig was employed through IBEW Local 481, putting his skills and training to work in a career he had worked hard to build. Away from work, Craig enjoyed the simple things, especially settling in to watch football. He was a lifelong and devoted Dallas Cowboys fan, faithfully cheering them on through every season.
More than anything, Craig was a beloved son, brother, uncle, nephew and cousin. His unexpected passing leaves an emptiness in the lives of those who knew and loved him, and he will be deeply missed by his family and those fortunate enough to have shared in his life. Craig is survived by his loving parents, Ronald M. and Peggy J. (Ray) Sethman of Shelbyville; sister, Denise M. (Eric) Bohnert of Lanesville; niece, Brooklynn Bohnert of Lanesville; nephew, Grayson Bohnert of Lanesville; aunts, Sandra (Robert) Motichak of Eighty Four, Pennsylvania, and Jeanne L. Boback of Columbus; stepgrandmother, Glenda Sethman of Millsboro, Pennsylvania; and cousins, Diane Ordich of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, Keith Boback (John-Michael Hendershot) of Columbus, Nicholas Motichak of Galloway, Ohio, and Christina Motichak of Erie, Pennsylvania. He was preceded in death by his paternal grandparents, Harold and Lillian Sethman; maternal grandparents, Robert and Rhea Ray; and several uncles.
The funeral service will begin at 2 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026, at Murphy-Parks Funeral Service in Shelbyville, with the Rev. Gretchen Schneider officiating. Visitation will also be Saturday at the funeral home from 11 a.m. until the time of service. Burial will follow at Forest Hill Cemetery in Shelbyville. Memorial contributions in Craig’s name may be made to the First Presbyterian Church Memorial Fund, 124 W. Broadway, Shelbyville, IN 46176. Please leave a fond memory of Craig at www.murphyparks.com or www.myersreed.com.
